strengths: Curates a large, diverse benchmark of 144 reasoning/planning tasks spanning math, spatial, logical, ordinal, optimization, and search reasoning, addressing a clear gap in prior tool-augmented RL work that focused narrowly on math or simple tool selection.

Proposes a novel multi-stage curriculum learning strategy guided by a principled 'improvement potential' metric (derived from multi-agent sampling), which is shown empirically to substantially boost RL gains (from +3.4% to +9.3%).

Strong empirical results: R1-CI-14B outperforms both GPT-4o (text-only) and GPT-4o with its native Code Interpreter despite being a much smaller open-source model, with consistent gains across 3B/7B/14B scales.

Includes a reasonably thorough theoretical analysis (variance/gradient bound argument) explaining why vanilla GRPO underperforms on heterogeneous task mixtures, connecting theory to the proposed curriculum design.
Useful systems contribution: a decoupled Code Execution Sandbox that reduces RL training time by ~39% by separating GPU gradient computation from CPU-based code execution.
Good set of ablations covering multi-turn vs single-turn CI framing, warm-start (SFT) vs cold-start RL, and Qwen-2.5 vs DeepSeek-distilled base models, which help isolate sources of improvement.
Interesting qualitative finding of emergent self-checking behavior via code generation after RL training, with a quantitative measurement of its increase.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Appendix C) rests on a simplified i.i.d. Bernoulli reward assumption and ignores PPO-style clipping and token-level advantage details, so it formalizes an intuitive/expected phenomenon (vanishing gradient at reward extremes) rather than providing rigorous new insight specific to the multi-turn/code-execution setting.

The improvement-potential estimation procedure itself requires substantial extra rollout computation (4 agent variants × 5 samples = 20 rollouts per sample) whose cost is not clearly incorporated into the reported training cost/efficiency analysis.

Evaluation pipeline relies on GPT-4o for answer normalization and for judging emergent self-checking behavior, which could introduce noise or bias that is not independently validated (e.g., via human annotation or inter-rater agreement).

Comparisons are largely limited to internal ablations (R1-CI variants) and GPT-4o; there is no direct empirical comparison against other recent tool-integrated RL methods (e.g., ToRL, ReTool, ToolRL) on the same 144-task suite, despite these being discussed extensively in related work.

No reported variance across multiple training seeds/runs, which is important given the acknowledged instability and sensitivity of RL training, especially with the multi-stage curriculum's fixed 150-step stage boundaries that appear empirically tuned rather than principled.
Only the Qwen-2.5 family is used as the primary base model line; generalization to other open model families beyond a single DeepSeek-distilled comparison point is not explored.
The abstract references dataset/code/model links that appear blank/missing in the provided manuscript, raising reproducibility concerns as presented.

Average accuracy numbers aggregate over highly heterogeneous tasks (144 tasks with very different difficulty and skill requirements), which may mask large per-task variance not fully analyzed beyond a coarse score-distribution figure.

strengths: Broad task curation across 144 diverse reasoning/planning tasks (SymBench, BBH, Reasoning-Gym) is more comprehensive than prior single-domain (math-only) tool-use RL work, and the tasks are standardized for automated rollout/evaluation.

The core empirical finding—that vanilla GRPO stalls on heterogeneous, mixed-difficulty multi-task data because policy gradient signal collapses when p(1-p)→0—is intuitive and reasonably well supported by the Fig. 3 ablations (single-task vs. many-task training curves).

The proposed improvement-potential-guided multi-stage curriculum is a sensible, lightweight fix, and the reported gains (RL lift from +3.4% to +9.3%) along with consistent improvements across 3B/7B/14B models suggest the method is not a one-off artifact.

Practical engineering contribution: decoupling code execution from GPU gradient computation via a CPU sandbox, yielding a credible 39% training-time reduction, is a useful systems contribution for the community.
Reasonably thorough ablations (multi-turn CI vs. single-turn text/code, warm start vs cold start, Qwen vs DeepSeek-distilled base) that isolate several design choices.
weaknesses: No direct empirical comparison against the most relevant prior RL+tool-use methods explicitly discussed in the intro/related work (ToRL, ReTool, ToolRL); the paper only compares against prompting baselines (All Text, All Code, CodeSteer) and an unfinetuned code agent, leaving the central claim of superiority over 'prior RL+tool-use efforts' empirically unsubstantiated.

Potential circularity/fairness issue: SFT data is synthesized by sampling and filtering GPT-4o trajectories, and the resulting fine-tuned model is then claimed to 'outperform' GPT-4o—this comparison conflates distillation from GPT-4o with an independent capability gain and is not adequately discussed or controlled for.

No variance/error bars, multiple seeds, or significance testing anywhere in the main results; the headline comparison (R1-CI-14B 72.4% vs. GPT-4o+CI 70.9%) is a small margin that could be within noise, undermining the strength of the 'outperforms GPT-4o+CI' claim.

The theoretical analysis (Appendix C and Sec. 4.2) rests on an elementary Cauchy–Schwarz bound on Bernoulli-reward variance; it is presented with heavy formalism (lemmas, propositions, 'rebuttal' sections) disproportionate to its actual novelty/insight, and does not account for clipping, which the paper itself acknowledges is omitted 'for analysis'.

Overclaiming of novelty: the paper repeatedly claims to be 'the first published work to train general Code Interpreter across multiple tasks and domains,' but curriculum learning by sample difficulty/variance and the p(1-p) intuition are well-established ideas in RL and active learning; the positioning overstates the conceptual contribution relative to engineering/empirical contribution.

Evaluation pipeline relies on GPT-4o for format normalization and for judging the 'emergent self-checking' behavior, introducing potential bias/noise into both the accuracy metrics and the qualitative behavioral claims, without any human verification or inter-rater reliability reported.

The improvement-potential estimation itself requires 20 rollouts (4 agents × 5 samples) per training question, which is a substantial additional sampling cost not clearly reflected in the reported GPU-hour training budget, making the true cost-efficiency claim incomplete.

Apparent overlap between this paper's CodeSteer baseline and the authors' own related prior work (Chen et al. 2025) raises questions about baseline independence/fairness, though not explicitly disclosed as a conflict.

Some tasks still score at or near zero even after the full training pipeline (Fig. 5), and the paper does not provide deeper failure analysis beyond a single anecdotal GPT-5 example, limiting insight into the actual robustness/generality of the approach.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: unlike prior tool-integrated RL work (ToRL, ReTool, ToolRL) restricted to math or simple tool selection, this paper trains a general-purpose Code Interpreter across 144 diverse reasoning/planning tasks spanning math, spatial, logical, ordinal, optimization, and search categories.

Strong empirical results: R1-CI-14B improves test accuracy from 44.1% to 72.4%, outperforming both text-only GPT-4o (58.6%) and GPT-4o with its native Code Interpreter (70.9%), despite using a much smaller open-source base model.

The multi-stage curriculum learning approach guided by 'improvement potential' (Πi = 4pi(1-pi)) is a sensible and well-motivated idea, supported by both empirical evidence (Fig. 3 vs Fig. 4) and a (though simplified) theoretical justification connecting reward variance to policy gradient magnitude.

Useful systems contribution: decoupling code execution from GPU gradient computation via a CPU sandbox yields a meaningful 39% training-time reduction, which is a practical takeaway for the community.

Extensive ablations covering warm vs. cold start, Qwen vs. DeepSeek-distilled base models, and multi-turn CI vs. single-turn All-Text/All-Code frameworks, which help isolate the sources of improvement.
Interesting qualitative finding of emergent self-checking behavior via code generation, quantified in Fig. 6a, adding some interpretability to the training dynamics.
Detailed task documentation (144 tasks described in the appendix) supports reproducibility and gives the community a potentially reusable benchmark suite.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis in Appendix C is fairly elementary (Bernoulli variance and Cauchy-Schwarz bound under simplifying assumptions like i.i.d. rewards and ignoring clipping) and largely formalizes an intuitive observation rather than providing deep new insight; framing it as a rigorous 'proof' may overstate its contribution.

Baselines are somewhat narrow: the paper compares primarily against GPT-4o (used to generate its own SFT data) rather than stronger/more recent frontier models or other open-source reasoning+tool-use systems, making it harder to assess how competitive R1-CI truly is against the current state of the art.

The 144 tasks, while diverse, are largely synthetic puzzle/algorithmic benchmarks (Reasoning-Gym, BBH, SymBench); it is unclear how well findings transfer to real-world, open-ended tasks requiring code use (e.g., data analysis, software engineering).

Key design choices such as curriculum stage length (150 steps/stage), reward weighting, and the number of stages (4) appear to be manually tuned without sensitivity analysis, raising reproducibility and generalizability concerns for other task suites or model families.

Correctness verification for self-checking code and reward computation relies on rule-based checks and GPT-4o-assisted normalization; potential reward-hacking or verification errors (e.g., a flawed verification script reporting 'Correct' incorrectly) are not analyzed.

Training cost remains very high (1845 GPU-hours even after the 39% reduction for the 14B model), which may limit practical reproducibility for many groups, and cost-effectiveness relative to gains is not deeply discussed.

Experiments are limited to Qwen-2.5 3B/7B/14B; no results at larger scale or with different model families (aside from one DeepSeek-distilled comparison) are shown, limiting confidence that the approach scales further.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored gap: training a general-purpose Code Interpreter-augmented LLM across a broad and diverse set of 144 reasoning/planning tasks, rather than narrow math-only settings as in prior RL+tool-use work (ToRL, ReTool, ToolRL).

The core methodological contribution (curriculum learning guided by measured 'improvement potential' rather than raw difficulty) is intuitive, clearly motivated by an accompanying theoretical analysis of GRPO's vanishing gradient signal on too-easy/too-hard samples, and is empirically validated (Fig. 4, Fig. 14).

Extensive and well-organized ablation studies: SFT vs no SFT (warm vs cold start), curriculum vs no curriculum, improvement-potential vs difficulty-based ordering, GRPO vs PPO vs Reinforce++, online vs offline curriculum scheduling, single- vs multi-turn frameworks, base model choice (Qwen vs DeepSeek-distilled), and SFT data design choices.

Strong empirical results across 3B/7B/14B model scales, with the 14B model outperforming GPT-4o with its native Code Interpreter despite being much smaller, and reasonable generalization shown on OOD benchmarks (GPQA, AIME, cross-benchmark transfer).
Practical systems contribution: a decoupled CPU-based code execution sandbox that meaningfully reduces RL training wall-clock time (39%), which is a useful engineering insight for the community.
Interesting qualitative finding of emergent self-checking/verification behavior via code generation, with some quantitative support (Fig. 6a).
Reasonable reproducibility effort: detailed task descriptions in the appendix, promised release of code/data/models, and full training hyperparameters provided.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Section 4.2 and Appendix D) is a fairly standard variance/Cauchy-Schwarz argument about Bernoulli reward group variance; while it supports the intuition, it is a relatively simple derivation dressed up formally, and relies on idealizing assumptions (token-level advantage broadcast, i.i.d. Bernoulli rewards) that are not rigorously validated against actual training dynamics beyond the single confirmatory experiment in Fig. 14.

Key baselines (Code Agent, CodeSteer) are drawn from the same research group's prior work, and the main strong external comparison is limited to GPT-4o and Qwen3-14B; broader comparisons to other contemporary reasoning/tool-use models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1, other open code-agent frameworks, o1-class models) are largely absent, limiting confidence in the claimed superiority.

The improvement-potential estimation procedure requires substantial additional rollout cost (4 agent strategies × 5 samples per question) prior to RL training, but this overhead is not quantified or included in the reported cost analysis (Section 5.4), understating the true cost of the proposed method.

The claimed novelty of being the 'first' general-purpose Code Interpreter trained across many tasks is somewhat overstated given that the task suite is an aggregation of three existing benchmarks (SymBench, BBH, Reasoning-Gym) rather than newly created tasks, and the core techniques (SFT+GRPO, curriculum learning) are combinations of well-established methods.

SFT data and correctness labels are synthesized/filtered using GPT-4o, which could bias the resulting model's behavior toward GPT-4o's stylistic and reasoning patterns and makes it harder to disentangle genuine capability gains from distillation effects.
Several reported findings (e.g., no response-length growth during RL, contra prior work) are only explained with post-hoc hypotheses without direct empirical verification.

Most results are reported as single-run scores without variance/error bars (except the OOD table with 3 runs), making it difficult to assess statistical significance of the reported gains, especially for closely spaced ablation comparisons (e.g., R1-CI vs R1-CI wo IP).

strengths: Large-scale, carefully curated benchmark suite of 144 reasoning/planning tasks spanning three existing benchmark families (SymBench, BBH, Reasoning-Gym), standardized into a unified evaluation format for rollout/testing — a useful resource contribution if released.

Extensive empirical ablations: curriculum vs. no curriculum, improvement-potential vs. difficulty-based ordering, SFT dataset design choices, warm vs. cold start, GRPO vs. PPO vs. Reinforce++, offline vs. online curriculum, Qwen vs. DeepSeek-distilled base models — this breadth of ablations is commendable and helps isolate the source of gains.
Consistent, sizeable accuracy improvements across 3B/7B/14B model scales, with the 14B model surpassing GPT-4o (text-only) and GPT-4o+Code Interpreter on the curated test tasks.

A practical systems contribution (decoupled CPU-based code execution sandbox) that yields a meaningful 39% reduction in RL training time, which is useful for practitioners replicating tool-augmented RL training.
Inclusion of some OOD evaluation (GPQA, AIME, held-out BBH) to partially test generalization beyond the curated task pool.
weaknesses: The headline 'theoretical analysis' in Sec 4.2/Appendix D essentially reformalizes the well-known fact that GRPO's group-relative advantage vanishes when all rollouts in a group share the same reward (p near 0 or 1); this is standard RLHF/GRPO folklore, not a novel insight, yet it is presented with heavy formalism (lemmas, propositions, 'descent lemma' arguments) that inflates the perceived technical contribution without adding new understanding.

The 'improvement potential' curriculum is essentially a success-rate-based (0.5-success) difficulty reweighting scheme; while the ablation vs. plain difficulty curriculum (R1-CI wo IP) shows some gain, the conceptual novelty over standard curriculum learning by pass-rate (used in several prior RL-for-reasoning papers) is limited and under-discussed relative to existing literature on curriculum/variance filtering for GRPO-style training.

No direct empirical comparison against the most relevant prior tool-RL baselines explicitly named in the paper (ToRL, ReTool, ToolRL) on the same task suite — these are only discussed qualitatively in Related Work, leaving the claimed advantage over 'narrow-domain' tool-RL methods empirically unverified.

The train/test split is only sample-level, not task-distribution-level: the 37 'test tasks' are drawn from the same three source benchmarks and likely share substantial skill/format overlap with the 107 training tasks, so the reported test gains may not reflect generalization to genuinely novel task types as strongly as claimed; the OOD evaluation (GPQA, AIME, held-out BBH) is comparatively limited in scope and partly reuses the same training benchmark family (BBH).

The 'emergent self-checking via code' behavior is framed as a novel finding ('rarely observed before'), but code-based self-verification with GPT-4 Code Interpreter was already documented in prior work (e.g., Zhou et al. 2023a); the paper does not adequately contrast its finding against this prior observation, overstating novelty.

Training cost is very high (1845 GPU hours for the 14B model even after the 39% sandbox speedup), raising reproducibility concerns for most academic groups, and the paper does not report variance across seeds/runs for most of its headline numbers (Table 3), making it hard to assess statistical reliability of the reported gains.

Reward design (format bonus, turn-count penalty) and evaluation reliance on GPT-4o for 'format normalization' introduce potential confounds/reward-hacking or evaluation noise that are not analyzed or stress-tested.

The multi-stage curriculum design (4 equal-sized groups, fixed 150 steps per stage) appears heuristically chosen without sensitivity analysis on the number of stages, group boundaries, or stage length, limiting confidence that the specific recipe generalizes beyond the studied setting.

strengths: Curates a large, diverse benchmark suite (144 tasks from SymBench, BBH, and Reasoning-Gym) spanning math, spatial, logical, ordinal, optimization, and search reasoning, unlike prior code-interpreter RL work restricted to math (ToRL, ReTool) or simple tool selection (ToolRL).

The core technical contribution -- multi-stage curriculum learning guided by 'improvement potential' Πi = 4pi(1-pi) -- is well motivated both empirically (Fig. 3, showing vanilla GRPO gains shrink from 27.4% single-task to 3.3% at 107 tasks) and theoretically (Appendix D provides a clean variance/Cauchy-Schwarz argument for why mixed-difficulty batches yield vanishing policy gradients).

Strong and consistent empirical gains across three model scales (3B/7B/14B): R1-CI-14B reaches 72.4% average test accuracy, beating both GPT-4o (58.6%) and GPT-4o+Code Interpreter (70.9%), and RL gains rise from +3.4% to +9.3% with the proposed curriculum.

Extensive and well-designed ablation suite: SFT dataset design choices, multi-turn vs single-turn frameworks, warm vs cold start, GRPO vs PPO vs Reinforce++, offline vs online curriculum variants, number of RL rounds, Qwen vs DeepSeek-distilled base models, and impact of potential range on training -- collectively giving good support to the design decisions.

Practical systems contribution (decoupled CPU-based Code Execution Sandbox) that reduces RL training time by ~39%, addressing a real bottleneck (Fig. 12 GPU utilization) relevant to the broader tool-augmented RL community.

OOD generalization checks (GPQA, AIME, BBH held out during training) show the trained models transfer beyond the curated task pool, partially addressing concerns about overfitting to the 144-task suite.

Interesting qualitative finding of emergent self-checking/code-verification behavior, quantified via GPT-4o-judged trajectory analysis (Fig. 6a), adding interpretability to the RL-induced behavior change.
weaknesses: SFT data is generated by GPT-4o and later compared against GPT-4o as a baseline; while the paper notes R1-CI surpasses its own teacher, the potential distributional/contamination effects of training on GPT-4o trajectories and then beating GPT-4o deserves more discussion.

Many Reasoning-Gym tasks (e.g., base conversion, letter counting, arithmetic, sorting) are close to textbook code-execution problems where a Code Interpreter trivially dominates; this may inflate aggregate gains and makes 'reasoning' claims partly conflate with 'exact symbolic execution' capability rather than reasoning per se.

The theoretical analysis in Section 4.2/Appendix D, while a nice sanity check, is a fairly simple variance bound under an idealized i.i.d. Bernoulli reward assumption and is presented with more formality (lemmas, propositions) than its actual novelty/rigor warrants; it does not by itself prove the curriculum is optimal, only that it targets higher-variance samples.

Improvement-potential estimation requires sampling 4 agent variants x 5 temperatures = 20 rollouts per training question before RL even begins, which is a non-trivial additional cost not clearly folded into the reported 1845 GPU-hour training budget.

Main results in Table 3 lack variance/error bars or repeated-run statistics (unlike the OOD table), making it harder to assess whether reported gains (e.g., R1-CI vs R1-CI wo IP) are robust to sampling noise.

Baselines against more recent strong general-purpose or reasoning models (e.g., only one comparison point with Qwen3-14B, no comparison to other contemporaneous open reasoning+tool models) are relatively limited, so the competitive landscape claim (outperforming GPT-4o+CI) could be strengthened with more contemporary baselines.

Task taxonomy and 'first general-purpose Code Interpreter' framing might be slightly overclaimed given concurrent related work is only lightly differentiated (e.g., rStar-Math, other multi-domain tool-RL efforts) beyond citation.
